problem: The definition 'Strain energy U is the elastic energy stored in a member when it deforms' has no elastic-limit restriction, yet every formula in the section (u = σ²/2E, U = P²L/2AE) is valid only while the material obeys Hooke's law. A student can carry these formulas past yield, which the traps later warn against but the definition does not.
fix: Strain energy U is the energy stored in a member deformed within the elastic limit; the formulas below hold only while Hooke's law is obeyed.

problem: 'Some syllabi call strain energy resilience' is loose. Textbooks define resilience as the strain energy stored up to the elastic limit, and proof resilience as the maximum such value at the limit; saying strain energy = resilience blurs the distinction made in the very next sentence.
fix: The strain energy stored up to the elastic limit is called resilience. Its maximum value, at the elastic limit, is the proof resilience: the largest energy the member can store without permanent set.

problem: The step 'P_max = 2W' silently assumes the weight is set on the member from rest, with zero initial velocity, at the undeformed position. A student who applies the same 2W/A result to a load arriving with any velocity gets an unsafe stress.
fix: Add: this result assumes the weight is released from rest at the undeformed position; if the weight arrives with velocity, the case is impact loading and the drop height h must be used.

problem: The label 'Static stress' is not defined in the example; a reader may read it as the stress at the final static equilibrium of the suddenly applied weight rather than the stress for the same weight applied gradually.
fix: Step 2: Static stress (the stress if the same 10 kN were applied gradually): σ_st = W/A = 33.33 MPa.
